en: Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Holy Ones. With firm limbs and bodies, having offered praise, may we attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods.

May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are uninjured, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ. Peace! Peace! Peace! Oṃ.

This is the *Atharvaṇa Upaniṣad*, beginning with "Brahmā, the first of the gods," and so forth. At the very outset, the text itself states the lineage (*paramparā*) characterized by the succession of those who established the transmission of this knowledge, for the purpose of praise. For, by thus [stating the lineage], it magnifies the knowledge—showing that it was obtained through great effort from a teacher as a means to the supreme human goal—in order to inspire the listeners' interest. Indeed, when knowledge has been made attractive through praise, people will engage in it with reverence.

However, he will later state the relationship between knowledge (*vidyā*) and its purpose in terms of the means and the end to be accomplished, beginning with the words, "The knot of the heart is broken. And here, having himself stated that in the lower knowledge—denoted by the word "lower"—which consists of the Ṛgveda and so forth and is devoted solely to injunctions and prohibitions, there is no capacity to remove defects such as ignorance (*avidyā*) which cause the need for purification, he first establishes the distinction between higher and lower knowledge through the passage beginning, "Remaining in the midst of ignorance," and likewise [describes] the means for attaining the Supreme.

The text declares the knowledge of Brahman—which is obtainable through the grace of the Guru and is preceded by detachment from all means of accomplishment and their objects—through the passage beginning with "Having examined the worlds. It repeatedly states the purpose [of this knowledge] in such passages as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" and "All, having reached the supreme immortality, are completely liberated. Although all those belonging to any stage of life (āśrama) are eligible for mere knowledge, the text shows that the knowledge of Brahman which is the means to liberation is rooted solely in renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and is not accompanied by ritual action (karman), by stating "wandering about on a mendicant's alms-round" and "by the yoga of renunciation."

And because of the contradiction between knowledge and ritual action. Indeed, it is not possible to perform ritual action even in a dream alongside the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self. Since knowledge is independent of specific time and has no fixed causal conditions, its restriction by time is untenable. As for the indicative marks found among householders—such as their acting as transmitters of the tradition of Brahma-knowledge—these are not capable of subverting the established principle. For even by a hundred injunctions, it is impossible to bring darkness and light into coexistence in one place; how much less so by mere indicative marks?

Having thus stated the connection and the purpose, the brief commentary on the text of this Upaniṣad is now commenced. It is called an *Upaniṣad* because it "shatters" (*ni-śātayati*) the multitude of misfortunes—such as conception, birth, old age, and disease—for those who approach this knowledge of Brahman with faith and devotion as their very self, or because it "causes them to go to" (*gamayati*) the supreme Brahman, or because it "completely brings to an end" (*avasādayati*) and destroys the cause of transmigratory existence, beginning with ignorance; for such is the traditional meaning of the root *sad* preceded by the prefixes *upa* and *ni*.

Om. Brahmā was the first among the gods to come into being; he is the creator of the universe and the protector of the world. He taught the knowledge of Brahman—the foundation of all knowledge—to Atharvan, his eldest son. 1.1.

Brahmā is the great sovereign, who surpasses all others by virtue of his righteousness (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). Being the foremost among the radiant gods (*deva*), such as Indra and others, he was born—that is, manifested—either as the first or at the beginning, being preeminent in his qualities due to perfect independence; this is the intended meaning. He is not like other transmigrating beings who are born under the influence of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*); for so it is stated in the Smṛti: "He who is beyond the senses, ungraspable... and so forth.

The creator and producer of the entire universe, and the protector and sustainer of the world that has been produced—these are epithets of Brahmā intended for the praise of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). He, Brahmā, whose greatness is thus renowned, [taught] the *brahmavidyā*, the knowledge of Brahman, the Supreme Self, by which one knows the Imperishable Person as Truth (*satya*); for that knowledge, concerning the Supreme Self, was indeed spoken by Brahmā, the first-born of speech. That is the *brahmavidyā*, and by means of this very knowledge, the reality that is to be known through all sciences is understood.

Thus, according to the Vedic scripture: "By this, the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known. And [the text] praises it as "the foundation of all knowledge. [Brahmā] spoke the knowledge to Atharvan, his eldest son. He is the eldest because he was created first at the beginning of one of the many modes of Brahmā’s creation; thus, he spoke it to that eldest son. (1.1)

The Brahmā taught that knowledge of Brahman which Atharvan had proclaimed to Atharvaṇa; he [Atharvaṇa] spoke it to Aṅgiras; and Bhāradvāja spoke that supreme and inferior knowledge to Satyavaha, the son of Aṅgiras. 1.1.2.

Brahmā taught this very knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), which he had obtained from Brahmā himself, to Atharvan; and in former times, Atharvan spoke—that is, declared—this knowledge of Brahman to Aṅgiras, who was named Aṅgiras. And that Aṅgiras spoke it to Satyavaha, a descendant of Bharadvāja belonging to the Bharadvāja lineage, whose name was Satyavaha.

Bhāradvāja spoke that which is "parāvarā"—meaning either that which was obtained from each successive predecessor by each subsequent successor, or that which pervades the entire range of higher and lower sciences—to his own disciple Aṅgiras, whether he was his son or not; the phrase "spoke to Aṅgiras" is to be supplied [to complete the sentence]. 1.1.2.
Śaunaka, a man of great wealth, having approached Aṅgiras in the prescribed manner, asked: "Venerable sir, when what is known does all this become known? (1.1.3)

Śaunaka—the offspring of Śunaka, a great householder (mahāśāla)—having approached the teacher Āṅgirasa, who was a disciple of Bhāradvāja, according to rule (vidhivat), that is, in accordance with the sacred precepts (yathāśāstram), and having thus arrived (upasanna), he questioned him (papraccha). Because of the specific mention of the relationship between Śaunaka and Āṅgirasa, it is understood that for those prior to this, there was no fixed rule regarding the rite of approaching a teacher. The qualification is intended either to establish a limit or to follow the "maxim of the lamp in the middle" (madhyadīpikā-nyāya); for the rite of approaching a teacher is also desired in the case of people such as ourselves.

He asks: "In what, O Blessed One? The word *tu* expresses a deliberation (*vitarka*). "O Blessed One," [he asks], "in what single thing, when known, does all this that is to be known become known—that is, specifically understood and comprehended? Having heard the traditional saying of the learned that "when one thing is known, one becomes a knower of all," Śaunaka, desiring to know the specific details of that, asked while deliberating, "In what, indeed? Alternatively, he may have asked out of common worldly observation, having already understood [the general principle].

In the world, there exist various distinct fragments such as gold and the like, which are recognized by worldly people through the single cognition of "gold-ness" and so forth. Likewise, is there perhaps a single cause for the entire diversity of the universe, such that when one thing is known, everything becomes known? [Objection: But surely, if it is unknown, the question "in what? is inappropriate; rather, the question "does that exist? would be appropriate. For only once existence is established can there be the question "in what?", just as one asks "on what is this to be placed? [Reply: This is not so. Just as in the case of a person who has lost a cow, the question "where is it? arises even though its existence is already established, so too, since the existence of the effect is already established by its being perceived, the question "in what is it supported? is appropriate. Furthermore, just as when a person who has lost a ring asks "where is it? and is told "it is on your finger," and upon seeing it there, he realizes "this very thing was the one I had lost," so too, when the existence of the effect is established, the question "in what is it supported? is appropriate. Because of the excessive length of the syllables and our fear of the iron [of punishment], we have fled; for in what single thing, when known, would one become all-knowing? 1.1.3.
To him he said: "There are two kinds of knowledge to be known," so indeed say those who know Brahman, "the higher and the lower. 1.1.4.

To that Śaunaka, Aṅgiras indeed spoke; what was said? It is stated: "Two sciences are to be known"—this is indeed what those who know Brahman, who are conversant with the meaning of the Vedas and perceivers of the supreme truth, have declared. What are they? He says: the higher (parā), which is the science of the Supreme Self, and the lower (aparā), which concerns the means and fruits of dharma and adharma. Now, Śaunaka had asked, "When one thing is known, does one become all-knowing?"—and while that [the means to all-knowledge] ought to have been explained, Aṅgiras instead spoke of the two sciences and so forth.

This is not a fault, because the reply depends upon a sequence. For there is another form of ignorance that must first be dispelled; for if its object were known, nothing would remain to be known in reality. This is according to the logical principle that the final conclusion (siddhānta) must be stated only after the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) has been refuted. 1.1.4.

Therein, the lower [knowledge] consists of the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, Atharvaveda, phonetics (śikṣā), ritual (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), prosody (chandas), and astronomy (jyotiṣa). Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is attained. 1.1.5.

In this context, what is called "lower" (aparā) knowledge? The *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*, the *Sāmaveda*, and the *Atharvaveda*—these are the four Vedas; and *Śikṣā*, *Kalpa*, *Vyākaraṇa*, *Nirukta*, *Chandas*, and *Jyotiṣa* are the six auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*). This is the lower knowledge. Now, this higher (parā) knowledge is described as that by which the Imperishable (*akṣara*), characterized as will be stated hereafter, is attained (*adhigamyate*) or reached. For the root *gam* preceded by *adhi* generally signifies "attainment. Furthermore, there is no difference between the attainment of the Supreme and the act of understanding; for the very removal of ignorance is the attainment of the Supreme, not something distinct from it.

[Objection: In that case, how could that [knowledge] which is outside the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas be the supreme knowledge (*parā vidyā*) and the means to liberation? For they remember in their tradition: "Those Smṛtis which are outside the Vedas, and whatever false views (*kudṛṣṭi*) there may be... Because it would be a false view and fruitless, it would not be acceptable. Furthermore, the Upaniṣads would then be outside the Ṛgveda and the others. If, however, they were part of the Ṛgveda and so forth, their separate mention would be purposeless; thus, it must be "supreme" (*parā*).

No; for what is intended here is the cognition whose object is that which is to be known. Indeed, it is the cognition whose object is the Imperishable (akṣara) to be known through the Upaniṣads that is primarily intended here by the term "higher knowledge" (parā vidyā), not the collection of words consisting of the Upaniṣads themselves. By the word "Veda," however, the collection of words is everywhere intended.

Even upon the mastery of the collection of words, the attainment of the Imperishable is not possible without further effort characterized by approaching a teacher and so forth, as well as dispassion (vairāgya); thus there is a separate treatment of the knowledge of Brahman and its designation as "higher knowledge. || 1.1.5 ||

Just as in the domain of ritual injunctions (*vidhi*), there exists an object to be performed subsequent to the time of knowing the meaning of the sentence—by means of the coordination of multiple factors such as the agent and so forth, characterized by the *agnihotra* sacrifice and the like—it is not so here in the domain of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*). Rather, [the realization] reaches its consummation at the very same time as the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence. This is because there is no state distinct from the mere knowledge of the object revealed solely by the words. Therefore, in this context, he qualifies the higher knowledge by means of the "Imperishable" (*akṣara*) with its attributes, beginning with "That which is invisible" (*yattad adṛśyam*). Having gathered what is about to be described within his intellect, he refers to it as if it were already established, saying "that which."

That which is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, devoid of eyes and ears, and without hands or feet; that which is eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, exceedingly subtle, and imperishable—into that as the source of all beings do the wise behold. 1.1.6.

"Undescribable" means invisible; that is to say, it is inaccessible to all the organs of perception (*buddhīndriya*), because the activity of the [external] sense of sight proceeds through the medium of the five senses. "Ungraspable" (*agrāhya*)—*gotra*, *anvaya*, and *mūla* are synonyms; thus "without lineage" (*agotra*) and "without succession" (*ananvaya*) mean the same thing. For there is no root for it by which it might be followed or succeeded. "Those which describe" are the *varṇas*, which are the properties of substances such as grossness and so forth, or whiteness and so forth. That in which these *varṇas* do not exist is the "colorless" (*avarṇa*) syllable (*akṣara*).

"Without eyes or ears, yet possessing both eyes and ears": for all living beings, these are the instruments regarding the objects of name-and-form (nāmarūpa). That [Being] in whom these do not exist is "without eyes or ears. Since the qualification "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" implies—just as in the case of transmigrating beings—that the accomplishment of purposes is achieved through instruments such as eyes and ears, that [notion] is here precluded by the statement "without eyes He sees, without ears He hears," as seen in such passages.

Furthermore, what is that which is "without hands or feet," meaning it is devoid of the organs of action? Since it is thus ungraspable and non-grasping, it is eternal and indestructible. It is "all-pervasive" (*vibhu*) because it exists in various forms (*vividham*) through the distinctions of living beings from Brahmā down to the stationary objects; thus it is all-pervasive. It is omnipresent and all-encompassing like space, and it is extremely subtle because it is devoid of the causes of grossness, such as sound and the rest. For sound and the others are the causes of increasing grossness in the sequence of space, air, and so forth; since those are absent, it is extremely subtle.

Furthermore, it is called "imperishable" (*avyaya*) precisely because its nature has been declared to be such; it does not perish. For in one who is bodiless (*anaṅga*), there can be no perishing characterized by the loss of one's own limbs, as there is in the case of a body. Nor can there be perishing characterized by the depletion of a treasury, as there is in the case of a king. Nor can there be perishing through the medium of qualities (*guṇa*), because [the Self] is devoid of qualities and is the self of all.

When the wise—the intelligent and discerning—behold this very characteristic as the source of beings, the cause of all creatures, like the earth is for the stationary and moving; when they behold it as the self of all, the imperishable (akṣara) everywhere, then that knowledge by which such an imperishable is attained is the supreme knowledge (parā vidyā). This is the collective meaning of the verse. (1.1.6)
It has been stated that the Imperishable is the source of beings. How is it the source of beings? This is explained by means of well-known illustrations:
"As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web], as herbs arise upon the earth, and as hair and body-hair grow from a living man, so does this entire universe arise here from the Imperishable. (1.1.7)

As is well known in the world: the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*), which is a silkworm, creates by itself—without depending on any other cause—threads that are not distinct from its own body; it extends them outward, and then, taking them back, it withdraws them and reduces them to its own being. And as on the earth, plants such as rice and others ending with stationary things arise; they emerge as non-different from their own self. And as from an existing, living person, hair and body-hair—which are of a different character—come forth.

Just as these have been illustrated, so too does the entire universe—the whole world—arise and originate here within the circle of saṃsāra from the Imperishable (Akṣara), which possesses the aforementioned characteristics and is both devoid of specific marks and yet endowed with its own essential nature, independent of any other cause. The employment of numerous illustrations, however, is for the purpose of easily awakening the understanding of the meaning. ||1.1.7||

The universe, which arises from Brahman, arises by this sequence and not simultaneously, like the scattering of a handful of jujube fruits; this mantra is commenced for the purpose of expressing the rule of sequence:
"By austerity, Brahman is built up; from that, food is born. From food arise life-breath, mind, truth, the worlds, and immortality in ritual acts. (1.1.8)

By means of austerity (*tapas*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and the understanding of the rules for manifestation, the Imperishable Brahman—the source of all beings—is accumulated and built up; desiring to bring this world-fetus into existence, it swells like a seed, as a father does with joy at the prospect of a son.

Thus, from that Brahman which has been augmented by omniscience and the specialized knowledge of the powers of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, there arises—that is, it is born—the "food" (*anna*): the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*) common substrate of transmigrating beings, which is called "food" because it is eaten and consumed. It is produced in the form of the state intended to be manifested.

And then, from that indeterminate food in its state of being about to be manifested, Hiraṇyagarbha—the vital breath (prāṇa), which is the soul of the world, presided over by the powers of knowledge and action of Brahman, and which is the sprout from the seed consisting of the aggregate of ignorance, desire, action, and the elements—is born; this is the syntactical connection.

And from that [Ākāśa], the mind—known as *manas* and consisting of volition (*saṅkalpa*), doubt (*vikalpa*), uncertainty (*saṃśaya*), and determination (*nirṇaya*)—is born. Furthermore, from that mind, which consists of volition and the like, "Truth" (*satya*)—the five elements beginning with space (*ākāśa*)—is born. From those five elements known as "Truth," the seven worlds, beginning with Bhūr, arise through the sequence of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*). Within them, there are the actions of living beings such as humans, according to the order of castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*). And when those actions serve as the instrumental cause, "Immortality" (*amṛta*)—the fruit born of action—arises.
As long as karmas do not perish even after hundreds of millions of eons, so long their fruit does not perish; thus [is] the nectar (amṛta). 1.1.8.
Desiring to conclude the very subject already discussed, the mantra states the following regarding the matter to be explained:
"He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge—from Him is born this Brahman, as well as name, form, and food. (1.1.9)

That which has been described by its characteristics as "the Imperishable" (akṣara) is the Omniscient One; he is "all-knowing" (sarvajña) because he knows everything in a general sense, and "all-perceiving" (sarvavit) because he knows everything in detail. From that aforementioned Omniscient One, whose austerity consists solely of knowledge—characterized by omniscience rather than physical exertion—this Brahma known as Hiraṇyagarbha, characterized as an effect, is born.

Furthermore, how is it that names such as Devadatta or Yajñadatta, forms such as white or blue, and food characterized by rice, barley, and so forth, come into being according to the sequence previously mentioned in the mantra? Thus, there should be seen no contradiction. (1.1.9)
Thus ends the first section;

now begins the second section. The Vedic sciences along with their auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) have been declared as the lower knowledge (*aparā vidyā*) by the passage beginning with "the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda," and so forth. By the textual portion beginning with "that which is invisible" and ending with "name, form, and food are born," the higher knowledge (*parā vidyā*)—characterized as the Imperishable (*akṣara*)—has been described with its specific qualifications, showing how it is attained through such knowledge. Hereafter, the subsequent text is commenced in order to distinguish the respective objects of these two types of knowledge: namely, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and liberation (*mokṣa*).

In this regard, the object of lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*) is *saṃsāra*, which consists of the distinctions between agents, means, actions, and fruits; it is beginningless and endless, and because its nature is suffering, it must be abandoned by each embodied being individually. In its totality, its connection is characterized by an uninterrupted flow like the current of a river.

Liberation (*mokṣa*), characterized by the cessation of that [saṃsāra], is the object of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*); it is beginningless and endless, free from old age, death, and fear, pure, serene, characterized by establishment in one's own Self, consisting of supreme bliss, and non-dual.

First, this [section] begins for the purpose of demonstrating the subject matter of the lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*), for when that is demonstrated, detachment from it becomes possible. And so he will say later: "Having examined the worlds acquired through action," and so forth. Indeed, examination is not possible unless the subject has been demonstrated; therefore, demonstrating it, he says: "This is the truth: the seers beheld in the mantras those rituals which were extensively propagated in the Tretā age. Perform them constantly, O you who desire the Truth; this is your path to the world of well-done deeds. (1.2.1)

This is true and not false. What is it? It is those rites, such as the Agnihotra and others, which the seers—the wise ones such as Vasiṣṭha and others—beheld (saw) within the mantras known as the Ṛgveda and so forth; and that which they beheld is this truth, because it is the exclusive means for achieving the goals of human life.

And those rites ordained by the Vedas and seen by the seers—which are characterized by the application of the three [Vedas], consisting of the offices of the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, and Udgātṛ priests, and which serve as the basis for ritual action—were practiced in many ways and in various forms, being performed continuously by ritualists; or rather, they were mostly set in motion during the Tretā age.

Therefore, you who desire the truth—desiring the fruits of actions as they truly are—should perform and carry out those [rites] constantly and with self-restraint. This is your path, the way for the sake of the world of the fruit of well-performed action—that is, the world which is seen, perceived, and enjoyed as the result of one's own performed deeds. The meaning is that this is the path for its purpose, for the attainment of that [world].
These rites prescribed in the three Vedas, such as the Agnihotra and others, are this path; the meaning is that they are the means for the certain attainment of their fruits. 1.2.1.
In this regard, first of all, the Agnihotra itself is described for the sake of illustration, because it is the foremost of all rites. How so?
"When the flame flickers in the kindled fire that carries the oblation, then one should offer the oblations between the two portions of clarified butter. (1.2.2)

When the fire, having been properly kindled with fuel added, is fully ignited and its flame flickers—that is, moves—at that time, while the flame is flickering, one should offer the oblations (āhutīḥ) between the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāgau), in the middle at the place of insertion, directed toward the deity; the plural "oblations" is used in view of the performance over many days. 1.2.2.

This path of action, characterized by the proper offering of oblations and so forth, is the way for attaining the worlds; yet its correct performance is difficult. Why? Because there are many failures. How so? "The world of one whose *agnihotra* is without the new-moon sacrifice, without the full-moon sacrifice, without the four-monthly sacrifices, without the *āgrayaṇa*, and devoid of guests; which is unoffered, without the *vaiśvadeva*, or offered contrary to rule—destroys his worlds unto the seventh generation. (1.2.3)

The *agnihotra* of one who maintains the sacred fires (*agnihotrī*) is "without the *darśa*"—that is, devoid of the rite known as the *darśa*—because the *darśa* is a duty necessarily to be performed by the maintainer of the sacred fires. Thus, the term becomes a qualifier of the *agnihotra*, as if it were an attribute related to the *agnihotra*. This refers to that [rite] being left unperformed. In the same way, the status of being a qualifier of the *agnihotra* should be understood in the cases of "without the *paurṇamāsa*" and so forth, since there is no difference in their being auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the *agnihotra*.

That which is "without the full-moon sacrifice" (apaurṇamāsam) means it is devoid of the full-moon rite; "without the four-monthly sacrifices" (acāturmāsyam) means it is devoid of the four-monthly rites; "without the Āgrayaṇa" (anāgrayaṇam) refers to that Āgrayaṇa rite to be performed in autumn and other seasons which is not performed by him; that in which the Agnihotra is offered correctly at its proper time by oneself; and that which is "without the Vaiśvadeva" (avaiśvadevam)—like the Darśa and others—meaning it is devoid of the Vaiśvadeva rite; even when being offered, if it is offered contrary to the rules, it is "not offered as prescribed" (na yathāhutam). Thus, what does such poorly performed or unperformed action—characterized here by the Agnihotra and other rites—accomplish? This is what is stated.

It "destroys," as it were, his worlds up to the seventh, including the seventh, because its fruit is merely exertion. For when rituals are performed correctly, the seven worlds beginning with Bhūḥ and ending with Satya bring forth their fruits in accordance with the transformation of those actions. However, by such [defective] acts as the Agnihotra and others, those very worlds—as they cannot be attained—become as if consumed; since only the mere exertion is invariably obtained, it is said that he "destroys" them.

Or rather, it is said that they are being destroyed because the fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons—who are connected through the favor of offerings of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth, and who constitute the seven worlds that benefit themselves—do not exist [in their true state] by means of the Agnihotra and other rites performed in the manner described. 1.2.3.
Kālī, Karālī, Manojava, Sulohitā, Sudhūmravarṇā, Sphuliṅginī, and Viśvarucī—the goddess flickering [with these] are the seven tongues of flame. 1.2.4.

"Kālī, Karālī, Manojava, Sulohitā, Sudhūmravarṇā, Sphuliṅginī, and the goddess Viśvarucī—these are the seven flickering tongues. Kālī and the others, ending with Viśvarucī, are these seven flickering tongues of Agni for the purpose of devouring the oblations offered. 1.2.4.
He who moves among these blazing fires, duly offering oblations, is led by these rays of the sun to where the sole lord of the gods has his abode. (1.2.5)

Among these various tongues of fire, the one who maintains the *agnihotra*—that is, the performer of the *agnihotra* and other rites—while they are blazing and shining, at the proper time—that is, at the specific time prescribed for each particular rite—the oblations offered by him, which are being taken up, lead him forward; that is, they cause him to reach that place. These oblations, having been offered by him, become the rays of the sun; the meaning is that they go by way of the rays. "Where" means in that heaven where Indra, the lord of the gods, dwells alone as the sovereign over all; thus he is called *adhivāsa*. (1.2.5)
How is it said that they carry the sacrificer by means of the sun’s rays?

It is said: "Come, come!"—thus do the resplendent oblations carry the sacrificer by means of the sun’s rays, addressing him with beloved words and honoring him, saying: "This is your holy world of Brahman, earned by meritorious deeds. (1.2.6)

"Come, come!"—thus calling out, they, being of beautiful luster and radiant appearance, and moreover addressing their beloved and desired speech characterized by praise and the like, uttering it and honoring [the path], [say]: "This is your meritorious, well-performed path, the world of Brahman (brahmaloka), which is the fruit [of your deeds]. The meaning is that they carry [the soul] along while thus addressing such beloved speech. From the context, "the world of Brahman" refers to heaven. 1.2.6.
And this action, devoid of knowledge and having such a limited fruit—the product of ignorance, desire, and action—is censured as being pithless and rooted in suffering:

"Frail indeed are these boats in the form of sacrifice, eighteen in number, wherein the inferior action is said to reside. Those fools who rejoice in this as the highest good go again and again to old age and death. (1.2.7)

The meaning is that they are "floating," which is to say perishable. For this reason, these eighteen—which are firm yet unstable, having the form of sacrifice (yajñarūpāḥ), meaning they are the forms of sacrifice or the performers of sacrifice—consisting of the sixteen priests, the wife, and the sacrificer, making eighteen in number; the scripture has declared that action (karma) rests upon these eighteen, wherein action is merely inferior, being devoid of knowledge.

Therefore, because those eighteen [elements] which serve as the substratum for inferior actions are unstable and floating, the action to be accomplished along with its fruit floats away; just as when a vessel is destroyed, the milk, curd, and other substances contained therein are destroyed.

Since this action leads to such a result, those undiscriminating fools who rejoice in it and look upon it with favor go again to old age and death—that is, having stayed in heaven for a short time, they return once more to this world. (1.2.7)
Remaining in the midst of ignorance, these fools consider themselves wise; being led astray, they wander about like blind men led by one who is himself blind. 1.2.8.

Existing in the midst of ignorance, being for the most part devoid of discrimination, they consider themselves to be "wise," "intelligent," "learned," and "those who have known what is to be known," thus esteeming themselves. Yet, being struck down—meaning they are violently afflicted and tormented by the multitudes of various evils such as old age and disease—they wander about in delusion.

Because they are bereft of vision, they are led along a path shown by one who is blind and sightless; just as people in the world who lack eyes fall into pits, upon thorns, and the like, so do they fall. 1.2.8.
Moreover:

"Fools, abiding in manifold ignorance, imagine themselves to have achieved their purpose; because those performers of ritual action do not understand out of passion, they fall down, their worlds exhausted. (1.2.9)

Existing in ignorance in many ways and in many forms, the ignorant—the foolish—conceive the conceit, thinking, "We alone have achieved our goal; we have accomplished our purpose. Because they, as performers of action, do not understand this reality and do not know it due to passion—that is, on account of being overwhelmed by passion for the fruits of action—for that reason, being afflicted and pained by suffering, their worlds are exhausted; having exhausted the fruits of their actions, they fall from the heavenly world. || 1.2.9 ||

Thinking that sacrifices and charitable works are the highest good, these deluded ones do not know any other excellence. Having enjoyed the fruits of their good deeds on the heights of heaven, they enter this world again or even one that is lower. 1.2.10.

Regarding *iṣṭa* as Vedic ritual such as sacrifice (*yāga*), and *pūrta* as Smṛti-based works such as the construction of tanks, wells, and ponds, they consider this alone to be the most excellent, the supreme, and the primary means for achieving the goals of human life; thus, being utterly deluded—infatuated with their sons, cattle, and kin—they do not perceive, that is, they do not know, the other means for attaining the highest good, which is called the knowledge of the Self.

And having experienced the fruits of their actions again and again on the back—that is, in the upper region—of Nāka, the heavenly world, as a locus for enjoyment, they enter this world, or one even lower than that, characterized by the state of animals, hell-beings, and so forth, according to the remainder of their karma. 1.2.10.

Those wise ones who dwell in the forest with austerity and faith, being tranquil and living on alms—freed from passion, they depart through the gate of the sun to where that immortal Person of imperishable nature resides. 1.2.11.

On the other hand, those who are the opposite of that—forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*) and renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) endowed with knowledge—they "dwell" in austerity and faith. Here, "austerity" refers to the action prescribed for one's own stage of life (*āśrama*), and "faith" refers to the forms of knowledge whose objects are Hiraṇyagarbha and others. Being established in the forest, they serve these two; being peaceful, their collection of sensory organs has ceased from activity. The meaning is that even householders who possess knowledge are primarily characterized by wisdom.

The connection is that those who practice the life of begging dwell in the forest because they lack possessions. By the "door of the sun"—meaning by the path characterized by the sun, namely the northern solstice—they, being "dustless" (virajas), which means their meritorious and sinful karmas have been exhausted, proceed; they go forth to where that Puruṣa resides, the first-born Hiraṇyagarbha, whose nature is imperishable (avyayātman) and who remains as long as saṃsāra exists.
These are the destinations within saṃsāra accessible through the lower knowledge.
Now, some indeed desire this to be liberation.

No, because of such scriptural passages as, "Right here all desires are dissolved," and "Having attained the All-pervading everywhere, the wise, with their selves disciplined, enter into everything itself," and because this is not the context [of the higher knowledge]. For since the discussion is proceeding under the section concerning lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*), there is no reason for liberation to be introduced abruptly. Furthermore, the state of being free from passion (*virajatva*) is merely relative. The entire sphere of activity of lower knowledge—characterized by means and ends, and divided by the distinctions of action, agent, and fruit—is precisely this much: that which culminates in the attainment of Hiraṇyagarbha.

And so it has been stated by Manu, while enumerating the courses of worldly existence beginning with the immobile beings: "The wise declare that Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest—this is the highest state characterized by sattva. (1.2.11)
Now, in order to demonstrate the qualification for the supreme knowledge in one who has become detached from this entire cycle of transmigratory existence consisting of means and ends, it is said:

"Having examined the worlds acquired through action, let the Brahmin attain detachment; there is nothing uncreated [eternal] to be gained by what is created. For the sake of realizing That, he should approach a Guru alone, carrying fuel in his hand—one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman. (1.2.12)

Having examined this—namely, that which falls within the scope of the lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*) such as the Ṛgveda and others; which is to be performed by a person naturally possessed of the defects of ignorance, desire, and action; which pertains to the sphere of ignorance because it is prescribed for a person who is indeed characterized by defects such as ignorance; and having examined those worlds which are its resulting effects, characterized by the southern and northern paths as fruits, as well as those characterized by hell, animals, and ghosts, which are brought about by the fault of failing to perform what is enjoined or transgressing prohibitions—by means of perception, inference, analogy, and scripture.

Having thoroughly ascertained from every perspective the worlds that constitute the course of saṃsāra—ranging from the unmanifest (avyakta) down to stationary objects, characterized by both the manifest and the unmanifest, serving as mutual causes for production like a seed and a sprout, crowded with hundreds of thousands of manifold evils, devoid of essence like the core of a plantain tree, resembling an illusion, a mirage, a city of Gandharvas, a dream, a water bubble, or foam, perishing at every moment, and brought about by merit and demerit accumulated through karma impelled by the defects of ignorance and desire—one should cast them behind one's back.

The mention of the "brāhmaṇa" is because the right (adhikāra) to the knowledge of Brahman through the renunciation of everything belongs especially to the brāhmaṇa. To the question, "Having examined the worlds, what should he do?", it is said: "disgust" (nirveda). Here, the root *vid* preceded by *nis-* has the sense of detachment; that is to say, one should attain detachment (*vairāgya*).

That mode of detachment is now demonstrated. In this world of transmigration, there is not a single object that is uncreated. Indeed, all worlds are accumulated through action (*karma*); because they are produced by action, they are impermanent. The intended meaning is that nothing whatsoever is eternal. Furthermore, every action is a means only for that which is impermanent, since all action consists of exactly four types of effects: that which is to be produced (*utpādya*), that which is to be obtained (*āpya*), that which is to be refined (*saṃskārya*), or that which is to be modified (*vikārya*). Beyond this, there is no further distinction of action.

I am one who seeks the goal that is eternal, immortal, fearless, immutable, immovable, and constant—not its opposite. Therefore, what is the use of performing action, which involves great exertion and is a means to what is not the ultimate goal? Thus despondent, the seeker should approach a Guru—that is, a teacher—who is endowed with tranquility, self-control, compassion, and other such qualities. Even though he may already know the scriptures, he should not seek knowledge of Brahman independently; this is the purpose of the restrictive emphasis "only a Guru."

With sacrificial fuel in hand—that is, with a bundle of firewood held in his hands—he should approach that teacher who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), perfected in the study and understanding of the scriptures, and established in Brahman—meaning one whose steadfastness is in the non-dual Brahman alone, having abandoned all ritual actions, just as one might say he is "steadfast in recitation" or "steadfast in austerity. For steadfastness in Brahman is not possible for one engaged in ritual action, because of the contradiction between the nature of action and knowledge. Having approached that teacher according to the prescribed rule and propitiated him, he should ask about the Imperishable, the Person, the Truth. (1.2.12)

To him who had approached him as a disciple, whose mind was perfectly tranquil and who was endowed with self-restraint, that wise one taught in its true essence that knowledge of Brahman by which one knows the Imperishable, the True Person. 1.2.13.

To him—who has approached, meaning who has come near; who is tranquil-minded, meaning whose defects such as pride have ceased; who is endowed with calmness (śama), meaning who is liberated through the withdrawal of the external senses; and who is possessed of dispassion toward everything—that wise teacher, a knower of Brahman, [should speak] properly, according to the scriptures.

By means of which consciousness and by which supreme knowledge one knows that very Imperishable (akṣara)—which is designated by the word *puruṣa* because of its fullness and because it dwells in the city (*puri*), which is the Truth (*satya*) because it is the ultimate reality, and which is the Imperishable (*akṣara*) because it does not perish, is undecaying, and is inexhaustible—one should proclaim that knowledge of Brahman as it truly is, exactly as it is.
This is the rule for the teacher as well: to rescue a worthy disciple from the great ocean of ignorance, as is required by right principle. 1.2.13.
The first *muṇḍaka* is completed.

The second *muṇṍaka*, first section: All that is an effect of the lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*) has been described. That cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), its essence, from which imperishable source (*akṣara*) it originates and into which it dissolves—that imperishable reality is called the Person (*puruṣa*). When that is known, all this becomes known; that is the subject matter of the higher knowledge of Brahman (*parā brahmavidyā*), and it is for this reason that the subsequent text is commenced.

This is the truth: just as from a well-kindled fire thousands of sparks of the same nature emerge, even so, my dear, various beings are born from the Imperishable, and into it they also enter again. 2.1.1.

That which is the object of lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*), characterized by the fruits of action, is relative truth; however, this [truth] is the object of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) because it is characterized as ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*). This very truth is the object of knowledge as it truly is, whereas the other is false because it is the object of ignorance (*avidyā*). Since [the Truth] is absolutely beyond the senses, how might people understand the imperishable (*akṣara*) Truth as if it were perceptible? To address this, he provides an illustration:

Just as from a well-kindled, brightly burning, blazing fire, sparks—parts of the fire—issue forth by the thousands in many ways, being of the same nature and possessing the very characteristics of fire; even so, O dear one, from the Imperishable (Akṣara) characterized as described above, various beings—that is, individual souls (jīvas)—which follow the distinctions of various limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as bodies, become manifold. Just as the various distinct cavities within space, though limited by adjuncts such as jars, experience their own particular divisions according to those adjuncts like jars, so it is here.

They are born following after the production of the limiting adjuncts of bodies created by name and form; and they go back into that very same Imperishable, merging as the limiting adjuncts of the body dissolve—just as the various cavities within a jar dissolve along with the dissolution of the jar itself.

Just as the cause of the production and dissolution of the various cavities in space is solely due to the limiting adjuncts such as jars, so too the cause of the production and dissolution of individual souls (jīvas) in the Imperishable is solely due to the limiting adjuncts of bodies created by name and form. 2.1.1.

Desiring to describe that which is beyond the "Imperishable" (akṣara)—which is itself other than the so-called "Indeterminate" (avyākṛta) that serves as the seed of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and is "other" (para) in relation to its own transformations—and which is the very nature of the Imperishable, devoid of all distinctions of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), like space devoid of all material forms, characterized by such attributes as "not this, not this" (neti neti), he says:
"For the divine Person is formless; He is indeed both within and without, unborn, without breath, without mind, pure, and higher than the high Imperishable. (2.1.2)

"Divine" means luminous, because it is self-luminous; or it exists in heaven, that is, within its own self, or it is worldly. For indeed, the Person (*puruṣa*) is formless, being devoid of all forms; he is full, or he dwells in the city (*puri-śaya*). "The divine Person is indeed formless," for he exists together with the external and the internal—that is, with both the outside and the inside. He is unborn, not born from anything whatsoever, because there is no cause for his birth other than himself; just as the sky is not the cause of the various cavities in jars and such things.

Since all modifications of existence have birth as their root, by the negation of that [birth], all [modifications] are negated. For he is both external and internal, unborn, undecaying, immortal, imperishable, and firm; this is the meaning.

Although, due to ignorance, those who perceive the distinctions of limiting adjuncts such as the body appear—as if possessing breath, mind, senses, and objects, like the sky appearing to possess dust, impurities, and so forth—nevertheless, from the perspective of the ultimate reality, it is "without breath" (*aprāṇa*), meaning that in it there exists no wind characterized by the differentiation of the power of action or consisting of movement; likewise, it is "without mind" (*amanā*), meaning that in it there exists no mind consisting of volition and so forth, which possesses the differentiation of various powers of cognition.

For it is said, "It is indeed without breath and without mind"; thus, the various winds such as prāṇa, the organs of action and their objects, as well as the intellect and the mind, along with the organs of perception and their objects, should be understood as being negated. Likewise, another Śruti states: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were."

And because He is thus devoid of the two aforementioned limiting adjuncts (upādhi), He is "bright" and pure. Therefore, in comparison to the Imperishable (akṣara)—which is characterized by the limiting adjuncts of name and form as the seed of all effects and instruments, and which is designated as the unmanifest (avyākṛta) and called the Imperishable because it is perceived as the seed of all modifications—the Person (Puruṣa) is "higher than the high Imperishable. The meaning is that He is the Person who is without limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika).

In that [Brahman] called Space, this imperishable which is the object of conventional usage is woven like warp and woof; how then is it said that it is devoid of vital breaths and so forth? For if the vital breaths and the rest existed prior to creation by their own nature, as they do in the case of a person, then the Supreme Person would possess vital breaths and so forth by virtue of those existing breaths. But those vital breaths and the rest do not exist prior to creation by their own nature, as they do in the case of a person; therefore, the Supreme Person is devoid of vital breaths and so forth, just as Devadatta is "sonless" before a son has been born. (2.1.2)
How is it said that breath and the others do not exist for him? Because:
"From this [Brahman] is born the breath, the mind, and all the senses; as well as space, wind, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe. (2.1.3)

From this very Person, characterized by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the seeds of name and form (*nāmarūpa*), there is born—that is, produced—the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of name and is of the nature of unreality (*anṛta-ātman*), being a modification within the sphere of ignorance (*avidyā*). This is because of another scriptural passage: "The modification is a mere handle of speech, a name; it is unreal. For the Supreme Self cannot possess the state of being "possessed of breath" through that unreal vital breath belonging to the sphere of ignorance, just as a man who has no son does not become "possessed of a son" by a son seen in a dream.

In this way, the mind, all the sense organs, and their objects are born from this very [Self]. Therefore, the meaning is that for the established [Self], the state of being devoid of vital breaths and so forth is non-figurative (literally: primary). And just as before creation they were non-existent in the ultimate sense, so too should they be regarded as having merged [into it] at dissolution.

Just as the instruments—the mind and the senses—so too are the elements the causes of the body and its objects: space (ākāśa), wind (vāyu) distinguished by its internal and external movements such as the "carrying" wind (āvaha), light (jyotis) which is fire (agni), water (āpas), and earth (pṛthivī), the sustainer of the universe and all things. These possess an increasing number of qualities—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—each accompanied by the qualities of those preceding it, and they are born from this very [Self]. 2.1.3.

Having briefly described the object of higher knowledge—the undifferentiated, true Person (puruṣa)—in the mantra beginning with "For divine, formless," etc., [the text] proceeds to explain that very same reality again in detail as possessing distinctions; for a subject matter explained both concisely and in detail becomes easy to comprehend, just like the statements in the Sūtras and their commentaries (bhāṣya). Furthermore, he says this to show that even Virāṭ—who is born from Hiraṇyagarbha, the first-born Prāṇa, and who is perceived as being separated by other principles within the cosmic egg—is born from this very Puruṣa and consists of Him. And he qualifies him: [The text continues: "From Him was born Virāṭ... and so forth. This is stated because, although Virāṭ is indeed produced from Hiraṇyagarbha, he is not distinct in essence from the Supreme Puruṣa; rather, he is manifested through the mediation of other principles. Thus, the text emphasizes that Virāṭ, though appearing as a separate entity, is ultimately non-different from the source of all. By describing him as "born from Him" and "consisting of Him," the author establishes his identity with the Supreme Puruṣa while acknowledging his manifestation as a specific cosmic form. This serves to remove any misconception that Virāṭ might be an independent principle rather than an emanation of the one True Being. Thus, the passage clarifies that the entire hierarchy of beings, including Virāṭ, is rooted in and sustained by the Supreme Puruṣa. This dual approach—first stating the truth in brief and then elaborating upon it—ensures that the profound nature of reality is accessible to the seeker. As the text further specifies, Virāṭ is characterized by his role as the progenitor of the physical universe and its inhabitants, yet his origin remains inseparable from the transcendent Puruṣa. This distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest is crucial for understanding the relationship between the individual soul (jīva), the cosmic soul (Hiraṇyagarbha), and the Absolute (Puruṣa). By defining Virāṭ in this manner, the author affirms the monistic foundation of the cosmos while providing a detailed map of its evolution. This method of exposition, moving from the abstract to the concrete, allows the student to grasp the unity of existence through its diversity. The subsequent verses will further elaborate on the attributes and powers of Virāṭ, demonstrating how the Supreme Puruṣa manifests through successive stages of creation. This progression from the unqualified (nirviśeṣa) to the qualified (saviśeṣa) is a pedagogical device designed to lead the aspirant toward a direct realization of the ultimate reality. Thus, the text concludes this section by reaffirming that all beings, from the highest deity to the lowest creature, are but expressions of the one eternal Truth. This comprehensive account ensures that the seeker does not mistake the phenomenal world for the ultimate reality, but perceives it as a reflection of the singular, undivided Puruṣa. Through this careful delineation, the author provides a complete picture of the cosmogonic process, grounding it firmly in the non-dual philosophy of the Upanishads. This approach is consistent with the traditional method of Vedāntic inquiry, which seeks to reconcile apparent contradictions by revealing the underlying unity of all existence. By explaining the birth of Virāṭ from Hiraṇyagarbha and tracing it back to the Supreme Puruṣa, the text removes any potential confusion regarding the status of intermediate deities and establishes the supremacy of the One without a second. This is the essential meaning intended by the author in this portion of the work. The qualification of Virāṭ serves to highlight his specific functions within the cosmic order while maintaining his ontological dependence on the Source. In summary, the passage demonstrates that the manifold universe, though appearing diverse, is in truth one with the Supreme Puruṣa. This realization is the goal of all spiritual practice. By following this path of understanding, the seeker attains liberation from the cycle of birth and death. Thus, the text provides a definitive explanation of the relationship between the Creator, the created, and the Creator of the Creator, establishing the foundational truth of the Upanishadic vision. This systematic presentation ensures that the profound teachings are not only intellectually understood but also spiritually realized. The author’s use of both concise and detailed descriptions is a hallmark of effective scriptural exposition, ensuring that the message is conveyed with clarity and depth. Through this method, the seeker is led from the known to the unknown, from the tangible to the intangible, until the veil of ignorance is pierced. This is the purpose of the sacred texts: to reveal the hidden truth of the Self. By following the instructions herein, the aspirant gains insight into the nature of reality and attains the state of eternal peace. This is the ultimate fruit of the study of the Upanishads. Therefore, the text concludes by emphasizing the importance of discerning the true nature of the Self beyond all names and forms. This is the core teaching of the scripture. By understanding this, one transcends the limitations of the ego and realizes one's identity with the Infinite. This is the final word of the author. All else is but an elaboration of this central truth. Thus, the passage stands as a testament to the power of the Upanishadic wisdom to transform the human mind.
