Agni is his head; the moon and sun are his eyes; the quarters of space are his ears; the Vedas are his opened mouth; Vāyu is his breath; the universe is his heart; and from his two feet the earth arose—for he is the inner self of all beings. (2.1.4)

Agni is the heavenly world, according to the Vedic scripture: "That world, O Gautama, is indeed Agni. His head is the highest limb, the crown of the head. "The moon and the sun are his two eyes"—this phrase is to be supplied everywhere; by changing the word "asya" (of him), which will be mentioned later, into "yasya" (whose). The quarters are his ears. His speech is the opened, manifest, and well-known Vedas. Vāyu is his breath.

The heart is the internal organ; "of whom" means of him whose universe—the entire world—is this [heart]. For the whole world is indeed a modification of the internal organ, since it is observed to dissolve into the mind alone during deep sleep, and even in the waking state, it is established from that very source like sparks from a fire. And he from whose two feet the earth was born—this god Viṣṇu is infinite, the first embodied being, having the three worlds as his bodily adjunct, and the inner self of all beings. (2.1.4)

For he is the seer, the hearer, the thinker, and the knower among all beings, the self that is the cause of all. And those creatures who transmigrate by way of the five fires are also said to be born from that very Puruṣa: "From him comes the fire whose fuel is the sun; from the moon, rain; from rain, plants upon the earth; the man pours his seed into the woman—thus many creatures are produced from the Puruṣa. (2.1.5)

From that Supreme Person arises Fire, which takes the form of the specific stages of the creation. It is further qualified: "the sun is its fuel. For it is by the sun that the heavenly world is kindled. From that, from the heavenly world once it has been produced, Parjanya—the second fire—comes into being. And from that Parjanya come the plants, which serve as the material cause for what is offered into the fire of the person. The male pours his seed into the female, into the woman, who is the fire of the woman.
In this manner, many, many offspring—beginning with the Brāhmaṇas—were produced and born from that supreme Puruṣa. ||2.1.5||

Furthermore, he says that the means of action and their fruits likewise arise from that alone. How so? "From that [arise] the Ṛg-verses, the Sāman-chants, and the Yajus-formulas; the initiations, all sacrifices, and the sacrificial fees; the year, the sacrificer, and the worlds; where Soma purifies itself, and where the Sun is. (2.1.6)

From that Puruṣa came the Ṛks—mantras characterized by specific meters such as the Gāyatrī, with fixed syllables, feet, and pauses; the Sāmans, consisting of five or seven musical divisions (bhaktis) and distinguished by musical modulations (stobhas) and the like; and the Yajus, which are in the form of prose sentences without fixed syllables, feet, or pauses. Thus, there are these three kinds of mantras. The initiations (dīkṣās) are characterized by the wearing of the girdle of muñja grass and other such marks, constituting specific rules for the performer. The sacrifices (yajñas) include all rites such as the Agnihotra and others. The sacrificial sessions (kratavas) are those accompanied by the sacrificial post (yūpa), and the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) range from a single cow up to the giving of one's entire property without limit.

And the year is time, which is an auxiliary to the ritual action. The sacrificer is the agent. The worlds are the fruits of his action, and they are specified as follows: those worlds in which Soma purifies—that is, purifies—while flowing, and those worlds where the sun shines; these are accessible by the two paths of the southern and northern solstices, and they constitute the fruits for the agents who are either ignorant or wise. 2.1.6.

And from that, the gods were produced in many ways—the Sādhyas, humans, cattle, and birds; as well as the out-breath and the in-breath, rice and barley, austerity, faith, truth, celibacy, and ritual ordinance. (2.1.7)

And from that Puruṣa, the gods—who constitute parts of ritual action—were fully produced in many ways according to the divisions of the classes of Vasus and others; as were the Sādhyas, a specific class of deities; humans, who are entitled to perform ritual actions; domestic and wild animals; birds; and the means of subsistence for humans and others, namely the out-breath and in-breath, and rice and barley for the purpose of oblation; and austerity (tapas), which is a part of ritual action characterized by the purification of the person, as well as being an independent means of attaining results.

Faith (*śraddhā*) is that which precedes the application of all means for achieving human goals; it is clarity of mind, a sense of conviction, as well as truthfulness—the avoidance of falsehood and speaking of things as they truly are—and non-inflicting [of harm]. Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the non-practice of sexual intercourse; and "method" (*vidhi*) refers to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). (2.1.7)

From Him the seven vital breaths arise; from Him the seven flames, the seven fuels, and the seven oblations. These seven worlds exist within which the vital breaths move—seven by seven, hidden and placed in the secret cave of the heart. 2.1.8.

The seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*) located in the head originate from that very Puruṣa. Their seven flames are the radiances that illuminate their respective objects. Likewise, there are seven fuel-sticks, which are the seven sense-objects; for it is by means of the objects that the vital breaths are kindled. There are seven oblations, which are the cognitions of those objects, according to another Vedic scripture: "That which is his cognition, that he offers as an oblation."

Moreover, there are seven worlds which are the stations of the senses, wherein the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) move and circulate. The phrase "wherein the vital breaths move" is an epithet of the *prāṇas* intended to exclude [the functions of] *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth. They are called "resting in the cave" (*guhāśaya*) because they lie within the cave—the body or the heart—at the time of sleep; they are placed and established by the Creator, seven for each distinct living being.

The meaning of this section is that all these—the actions of those who sacrifice for themselves and possess knowledge, as well as the fruits of their actions; and the actions of those who lack knowledge, along with the means for those actions and their fruits—all this has been produced from the Supreme Person alone, the Omniscient One. (2.1.8)
From him all the oceans and mountains arise, and from him flow all rivers of every form; from him come all herbs and juices, by which this inner self (antarātman) exists within these beings. 2.1.9.

From this Puruṣa come all the oceans, beginning with the salt ocean; from this very Puruṣa come all the mountains, beginning with the Himavat. From this very Puruṣa flow all the rivers and streams, such as the Gaṅgā and others, in all their forms and manifold varieties. From this very Puruṣa come all herbs, such as rice and barley, and the sixfold taste, beginning with sweet, by which [taste] the subtle body—the *liṅga*—remains enveloped by the five gross elements.
For that is called the "inner self" (*antarātmā*) because it exists within the interval between the body and the Self, acting as the Self's support. (2.1.9)

Thus, all this has come forth from the Person (Puruṣa). Therefore, modification is a mere beginning in speech, a name, and unreal; the Person alone is real. Hence: "The Person alone is this universe—action, austerity, Brahman, and the supreme immortal. He who knows this, hidden in the secret cave of the heart, O dear one, unravels the knot of ignorance in this very world. (2.1.10)

The Puruṣa alone is all this universe. There is nothing whatsoever called the universe that exists apart from the Puruṣa. Therefore, what was previously asked—"O Venerable One, when what is known does all this become known?"—is here stated: for when this supreme Self, the Puruṣa who is the cause of all, is known, it becomes known that "this universe is indeed the Puruṣa; there is nothing else."

What, then, is this "universe" that is spoken of? It is said to be action characterized by the Agnihotra and other rites; austerity; knowledge; the fruit produced by those; and all else—this much indeed is everything. And all this is the effect of Brahman. Therefore, he who knows that "I am indeed all this, the supreme immortal Brahman," scatters—that is, disperses and destroys—the latent impressions of ignorance which have become as firm as a knot, even while living here and not after death, O gentle one of pleasing appearance! 2.1.10.
Thus ends the first section.
Now, the second section begins:
it is stated how that which is formless and imperishable is to be known.

Manifest and yet hidden, moving in the cave [of the heart], this great state is established right here. This is that which breathes and blinks; know this as being both the existent and the non-existent, the most desirable, the supreme beyond understanding, and the highest among all creatures. 2.2.1.

It is manifest (*āviḥ*), luminous, and present; for according to another scriptural passage, it shines forth as one perceives sound and the other objects of sense through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of speech and so on. It is perceived within the hearts of all living beings as the Reality (*sat*) manifested through the attributes of the limiting adjuncts such as seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing. This very Brahman, which is manifest and perfectly situated within the heart, is called "moving in the cave" (*guhā-cara*); it is renowned as moving in the cave because it moves within the cave by way of seeing, hearing, and so forth. It is "Great" (*mahat*) because of its being greater than all. It is the "Abode" (*padam*) because it is reached by everyone, as it is the locus of all objects of experience.

How is that state called "great"? Because in this Brahman all this is deposited—that is, inserted like spokes in the hub of a chariot wheel—whatever moves or is mobile, such as birds and the like; whatever breathes or lives, such as humans, animals, and so forth, characterized by the vital breaths of prāṇa and apāna; and whatever blinks or performs actions, including even that which does not blink—all this, in its entirety, is deposited right here in Brahman.

O disciples, know and understand that this entire world has its foundation therein; it is the very self of yours, being the nature of both the existent and the non-existent. This is because, apart from it, there is no existence of either the existent or the non-existent, nor of the formed or the formless, nor of the gross or the subtle. It is "vareṇya," meaning worthy of being chosen, for it alone is to be prayed for by all because of its eternity. It is "para," distinct; this connects with the word "vijñāna" (knowledge) which is separated [in the verse], meaning that it is beyond the scope of ordinary worldly knowledge.
That which is the most excellent, the best among all things that are excellent—that indeed is the one Brahman, pre-eminently excellent because it is free from all defects. (2.2.1)
Moreover:

That which is luminous, subtler than the subtle, in which the worlds and the inhabitants of the worlds are contained—that is this Imperishable Brahman; it is life-breath, it is speech, it is mind; it is the Real, it is the Immortal; that, O dear one, you must pierce—know that! 2.2.2.

That which is radiant and glowing—indeed, it is the luminous Brahman, for by its light the sun and other celestial bodies shine. Furthermore, that which is subtler than the minute, such as the *śyāmāka* grain and so forth; and by the word "also," it is understood that it is also exceedingly grosser than the gross, such as the earth and so forth. In that [Brahman] the worlds, beginning with the earth (*bhūr*), are placed and abide, as well as the inhabitants of those worlds, such as humans and others, all of whom are well known to have consciousness as their support.

This very imperishable Brahman is the support of all; it is that vital breath (prāṇa), and it is speech and mind—both speech and mind, as well as all the organs, and within them consciousness. For the entire aggregate of the vital breath, the senses, and so forth, has consciousness as its support, according to another scriptural text: "The breath of the breath.

That imperishable consciousness which lies within the vital breath and the rest is this Truth, which is non-false, therefore immortal and indestructible. It is to be pierced—that is, it is to be struck with the mind; the meaning is that one should practice concentration of the mind upon it. Therefore, my dear, knowing this, fix your consciousness on the Imperishable. 2.2.2.
How it is to be pierced is stated:

"Having taken up the great bow of the Upaniṣads, one should fix the arrow sharpened by meditation. Drawing that [bow] with a mind absorbed in That, O dear one, know that very Imperishable as the mark. (2.2.3)

Having taken up the bow, which is the seat of the arrow, one should join the arrow—that great weapon (mahāstra) which is well-known as being "pertaining to the Upaniṣads" (aupaniṣada), meaning it arises from the Upaniṣads—to that bow. To what is it like? He says: "sharpened by meditation" (upāsāniśitam), meaning refined and honed by continuous contemplation. Having joined [the arrow], one should draw it back; that is to say, having withdrawn the internal organ along with the senses from their respective objects and directed them toward the target alone.

For here, the drawing of a bow is not possible by means of the hand alone. "Bhāva" (being) is the mental cultivation directed toward that target, the Imperishable Brahman; with the mind absorbed in That, O dear one, know that very target to be the Imperishable characterized as previously described. 2.2.3.
Regarding that which was mentioned as the bow and so forth, it is said:

"The syllable Om (praṇava) is the bow, the self is indeed the arrow, and Brahman is declared to be its target. With undistracted mind, one must pierce it; like the arrow, one becomes absorbed in That. (2.2.4)

The *praṇava*, the syllable *oṃ*, is the bow. Just as a bow is the cause for the entry of an arrow into its target, so too is the *oṃ* the cause for the entry of the arrow that is the Self into the target that is the Imperishable (*akṣara*). For when one practices with the *praṇava*, being refined by it, one becomes established in the Imperishable through the non-obstruction of that support, just as an arrow shot from a bow enters its target. Therefore, the *praṇava* is like a bow; hence it is called the "bow."

For the arrow, characterized by the adjuncts of the self, has indeed entered here into the body as the very Supreme, like the sun in water, acting as the witness of all mental cognitions. Since that arrow is, as it were, fixed within its own self in the imperishable Brahman, Brahman is therefore called the "target" (lakṣya). This is because it is perceived as the target through the state of the Self by those desiring to concentrate their minds upon it, just like a target [is perceived].

This being so, one who is vigilant—free from the heedlessness of craving for the perception of external objects, detached from everything, with senses conquered and mind one-pointed—must pierce the target that is Brahman. Thereafter, by virtue of that piercing, one should become identical with That, like an arrow. The meaning is that just as the result of an arrow is its becoming one with the target, so too, by setting aside the notion of the self in the body and so forth, one should achieve the result of becoming one with the Imperishable. 2.2.4.
Because the Imperishable is indeed difficult to perceive, it is stated again and again for the sake of easy perception:

"In whom heaven and earth, as well as the intermediate space, and the mind together with all vital breaths are woven—know Him alone as the one Self; abandon other words; He is the bridge to immortality. (2.2.5)

O disciples, know that very One who is the support of all, the non-dual Second, in whom as the Imperishable Person heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven and established, along with the mind together with the vital breaths and all other instruments—know Him as the Self, the inward-facing reality of yourselves and of all living beings. Having known Him, abandon, utterly renounce, all other speech consisting of ignorance, and all action along with its means which is to be illuminated by that knowledge.

Since this is the bridge to immortality—this knowledge of the Self being like a bridge for the attainment of immortality, that is, liberation, because it is the cause for crossing over the great ocean of saṃsāra—so too says another Śruti: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey. (2.2.5)
Moreover:

"In whom the channels converge like the spokes in the hub of a wheel—he moves within, being born in many ways. Meditate upon the Self as 'Om' alone; may there be well-being for you to reach the further shore beyond darkness. (2.2.6)

Just as spokes are fixed in the nave of a wheel, so too are they gathered together and enter into that heart where all the nerves (nāḍīs) pervading the body converge; in that heart, this very Self under discussion, being the witness of the cognitions of the intellect, moves—meaning it dwells and functions—in the interior.

Seeing, hearing, thinking, and cognizing in many ways and various manners, as if being born through the notions of anger, joy, and so forth—though not actually born because it conforms to the limiting adjuncts of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—ordinary people say of that Self, "He has become joyful," or "He has become angry. Meditate upon that Self with the syllable *Oṃ* as your support, using the aforementioned method of contemplation; that is, reflect upon it.

The teacher, being knowledgeable, has said what was to be said to the disciples. And the disciples, desiring to know the knowledge of Brahman, have ceased from ritual action and have set out upon the path to liberation. For their attainment of Brahman to be free from obstacles, the teacher offers this benediction: "May there be well-being—may there be freedom from obstacles—for you, for the sake of reaching the further shore. Why is it called "the further shore"? It is because it lies beyond the darkness of ignorance; the meaning is that it is for the purpose of attaining the true nature of the Self as Brahman, which is devoid of ignorance. (2.2.6)

He who is beyond darkness, whom one must reach after crossing the great ocean of saṃsāra—that which is the object of higher knowledge—where does he abide? To this he says: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving; whose glory is on earth; he, the Self, is established in the divine city of Brahman, in the ether. Consisting of mind, the leader of the body of vital breath, he is established having placed his seat in the heart. By perceiving that, the wise behold the immortal form of bliss which shines forth. (2.2.7)

He who has been described as all-knowing (*sarvajña*) and all-perceiving (*sarvavit*) is further qualified by this: "Whose is this well-known majesty (*mahimā*), that is, power (*vibhūti*"? What is this majesty? It is that under whose command these two, heaven and earth, remain held apart; by whose command the sun and moon revolve incessantly like the wheels of a chariot; by whose command the rivers and the ocean do not overstep their own domain; and likewise, both the stationary and the moving, which remain fixed under his command.

Likewise, he is the one whose command the seasons and the years do not transgress; likewise, he is the one by whose command agents, actions, and their fruits do not overstep their respective times. This is the majesty upon the earth in this world. He is the Omniscient One, the God of such majesty, in the divine, luminous City of Brahman—the "City of Brahman" being so called because it is eternally manifest as the very nature of consciousness (brahman); that City of Brahman is the lotus of the heart, and within it is the space (vyoman).

In that sky, which is situated within the lotus of the heart, he is perceived as if established there; for it is not possible for one who is all-pervading like space to have going, coming, or staying in any other way. That Self, being situated there, is manifested solely through the activity of the mind; thus He is "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) because of having the mind as His limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). He is the "leader of the body and the vital breaths" (*prāṇa-śarīra-netā*); "body and vital breaths" means the physical body and the vital breaths, and He is their leader from this gross body to another body.

Having established and fixed his heart—his intellect—within the opening of the lotus of the heart, [he remains] while the food being consumed undergoes transformation day by day, and while the food in the form of a physical mass is increasing and decreasing. For the stationing of the Self is indeed its abiding in the heart; the stationing of the Self is not in the food.

The wise—the discerning ones—behold that reality of the Self, which is full in every respect, by means of distinguished knowledge produced through the instruction of the scriptures and teachers, arising from tranquility, self-control, meditation, total renunciation, and dispassion; they perceive and attain it as the form of bliss, free from all misfortune, suffering, and exertion, the immortal which shines forth preeminently, shining eternally within its own self alone. (2.2.7)
The fruit of this knowledge of the Supreme Self is declared as follows:
"The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut away, and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. (2.2.8)

The knot of the heart is severed—the accumulation of the latent impressions of ignorance (avidyā-vāsanā) which rests upon the intellect (buddhi) and constitutes desire, as another Vedic text states: "He in whose heart desires reside. This [desire] has the heart as its locus, not the Self; it is severed, meaning it undergoes dissolution. All doubts concerning the objects of all that is to be known cease; those doubts which have proceeded like the current of the Ganges until death come to an end.

For this one whose doubts have been severed and whose ignorance has ceased, those karmas that existed prior to the arising of knowledge—whether belonging to previous births with results yet to be experienced, or co-existent with the arising of knowledge—are destroyed. However, those karmas which initiated this present birth are not destroyed, because their results have already begun to manifest. When that omniscient one—the source and the effect, the higher and the lower (*parāvara*)—is seen directly as "I am He," one is liberated through the destruction of the cause of transmigratory existence; such is the meaning. (2.2.8)
The following three verses also provide a concise statement of the very same meaning already expressed:
"In the supreme golden sheath is the stainless, partless Brahman; that is the pure light of lights, which those who know the Self recognize. (2.2.9)

In that supreme sheath—which is golden, consisting of light, the radiance of intellectual discernment, and which is like the scabbard of a sword because it is the locus for perceiving the true nature of the Self—that Brahman is stainless, being free from the impurity of all defects such as ignorance and the rest. It is "supreme" because it is within everything, and it is "stainless" (*viraja*) because it is devoid of the dust and stain of all faults like ignorance. It is "without parts" (*niṣkala*), meaning that from it all parts (*kalā*) have departed; the sense is that it is without constituent members.

Because it is stainless and partless, that light is pure and shines even upon the lights—the fire and others—which are themselves the nature of all illumination. The meaning is that even the luminosity of fire and the other elements is caused by the light of the consciousness of the Brahman-Self residing within them.

For that indeed is the supreme light which is not illumined by anything else; it is the light of the Self. Those who are discriminative—the knowers of the Self—who know the Self as the ether (the witness of the intellect, its cognitions, and objects such as sound), they are the knowers of the Self; following the realization of the Self, they know that which is the supreme light. Therefore, they alone know it, and not others who follow the cognitions of external objects. 2.2.9.

How is it said that "He is the light of lights"?—There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. Everything shines only after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined. 2.2.10.

In that Brahman, which is one's own self, even the sun—which illuminates everything—does not shine; the meaning is that Brahman does not manifest by means of it. For it is by the light of Brahman alone that everything else, the entire collection of non-self, is illuminated; it has no inherent power of illumination of its own. Likewise, neither the moon nor the stars shine, nor do these lightnings, much less this fire within our sensory range. What more need be said? Whatever shines in this world shines only because that Supreme Lord Himself shines, for He is by nature the embodiment of light.

That which is shining makes other things shine and shines after them; just as water, a firebrand, and the like, by contact with fire, burn along with the burning fire but not by themselves, so too, by its own light, all this world, beginning with the sun, shines.

Since this is so, that very Brahman both shines and radiates through its various manifestations existing within its effects; thus, Brahman’s nature as light is understood from itself. For an illumination that exists inherently cannot produce the shining of another; for we do not observe objects such as jars to be illuminators of other things, whereas we do observe those whose nature is light, such as the sun and the like, to be so. (2.2.10)

That which is the light of lights, Brahman—that alone is the Truth; all else is its modification, a mere beginning in speech, a modification that is a mere name, while everything else is unreal. Having established this point at length through reasoning, the text concludes once more with a mantra serving as a summary: "Brahman alone is this immortal reality in the east; Brahman is behind, and Brahman is to the south and to the north. Pervaded by Brahman below and above, this entire universe is indeed Brahman, the most excellent. (2.2.11)

This which has been described by the aforementioned characteristics is Brahman alone. That which was previously, at the beginning, Brahman alone appearing as such to those with the vision of ignorance—likewise behind, likewise to the south, likewise to the north, and likewise below and above—it has extended and spread out everywhere as if it were something else, through the form of its effects, appearing as if possessed of name and form. What more need be said? Brahman alone is this entire universe, this most excellent and supreme world.
Every cognition of what is not Brahman is mere ignorance, like the cognition of a snake in a rope; "Brahman alone is the one ultimate reality"—this is the teaching of the Veda. 2.2.11.
This second Muṇḍaka is completed.
The Third Muṇḍaka—First Section.

The higher knowledge has been described by which that Imperishable, called the Puruṣa, the Truth, is attained; upon the attainment of which there occurs the absolute destruction of the cause of transmigratory existence, such as the knots of the heart and so forth. And the means for perceiving That—Yoga—has been explained through the metaphor of employing the bow and other implements. Now, the auxiliary means, such as the observances (satya) and others, must be stated; for this purpose, the subsequent section begins. Furthermore, the determination of the reality is carried out once more by another method, because it is exceedingly difficult to comprehend even when [previously] established.
In this regard, the mantra that serves as the aphorism is presented for the purpose of determining the ultimate reality:
"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating. (3.1.1)

"Two birds, two beautiful-winged ones (suparṇau)—either because they possess beautiful flight or because they share the common nature of birds—possessing beautiful wings; joined together (sayujau), always united; friends (sakhāyau), having a common designation and a common cause for manifestation—being such, they both embrace the same tree, which is undifferentiated as the locus of perception, like a single tree, because it shares the common nature of being subject to felling; that is, they cling to the body, which is like a tree, just as two birds might cling to one tree for the sake of enjoying its fruit."

For this tree has its roots upward and its branches downward; it is the sacred fig tree (aśvattha) whose origin is the unmanifest, which is designated as the field (kṣetra), and which is the substratum for the fruits of the actions of all living beings. Enveloping it are the two—the individual self (ātman) and the Lord (īśvara)—who, like two birds, have as their limiting adjuncts the subtle body (liṅga) that serves as the substratum for primordial desires, actions, and latent impressions.

Of those two who are embraced together, one—the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field)—residing in the tree of the limiting adjunct (*liṅga-upādhi*), eats the sweet fruit produced by action, which consists of pleasure and pain and is of the nature of various manifold experiences; he eats it, consumes it, and enjoys it due to a lack of discrimination. The other, the Lord (*īśvara*), does not eat; He is the other, whose nature is eternally pure, enlightened, and liberated, the omniscient Lord who possesses all beings as His limiting adjuncts.

For he is the impeller of both the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer, solely by virtue of his existence as the eternal witness. "But he, not eating, shines forth as another; he merely sees. Indeed, his role as impeller consists in mere seeing, like that of a king. (3.1.1)
This being so, it is said:

"Upon that very same tree, a person is immersed and grieves, deluded by his own lack of sovereignty. But when he beholds the other, the Lord, as one who is adored, and perceives His majesty, he becomes free from sorrow. (3.1.2)

In the "common tree" as previously described—the body—the person, the experiencer, the living soul (*jīva*), is overwhelmed by the heavy burden of ignorance, desire, the fruits of karma, and passion; like a gourd submerged in the waters of the ocean, it has certainly attained the state of identifying with the body. It gives rise to such notions as "I am this very one," "I am the son of so-and-so," "I am the grandson of so-and-so," "I am thin," "I am stout," "I am virtuous," "I am devoid of qualities," "I am a friend," or "I am miserable. It thinks, "There is no other besides me," and thus it is born, it dies, and it is joined with kinsmen and relatives.

Due to such powerlessness, no one is capable [of averting it]; thinking, "My son is lost, my wife is dead, what is the use of my life?"—thus, through that state of helplessness, he grieves and suffers, becoming bewildered by many kinds of misfortunes and falling into anxiety due to a lack of discernment.

Having thus undergone the state of constant wandering through the wombs of hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and so forth, at some point—due to the cause of having accumulated pure dharma over many births—he is shown the path of yoga by someone supremely compassionate. Endowed with non-violence, truthfulness, celibacy, total renunciation, tranquility, self-restraint, and other virtues, his self being concentrated, he [attains] that which is cherished.

When, at whatever time, having practiced many paths of yoga and various disciplines, one perceives through meditation this Lord—who is distinct from the characteristics of limiting adjuncts such as the tree, who is non-transmigratory, and who has transcended hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death—as the Self of all this world, thinking "I am He," equal to all, dwelling in all beings, and not the other [limited self] which is a mere illusory self partitioned by adjuncts born of ignorance; and when one thus sees His glory and majesty—that form of the universe belongs to Me alone, the Supreme Lord—then [one attains liberation].
"He becomes free from sorrow" means he is liberated from the entire ocean of grief and has accomplished all that was to be done. ||3.1.2||
Another mantra also expresses this very same meaning in detail:

"When the seer sees the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman; then the knower, shaking off both merit and demerit, becomes stainless and attains supreme equality. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.3)

When—at which time—the seer, meaning the wise practitioner who sees, beholds—as previously described—the golden-hued one whose nature is self-luminous, or whose light is like that of gold, the indestructible agent of the entire world, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman (brahmayonim)—meaning he whose source is Brahman, or the source of the other Brahman—then that wise seer, having shaken off both merit and demerit, which are the roots of bondage consisting of karma, [is liberated].

Having cast off and burned away [all taints], being stainless, untainted, and free from afflictions, he attains—reaches—the supreme, most excellent, unsurpassed equality, which is characterized by non-duality. Since all objects of duality are generally inferior, this supreme equality is characterized by non-duality. ||3.1.3||
Moreover:

"For he is indeed the vital breath who shines forth through all beings; the one who knows thus becomes a wise man who does not speak of transcendence. He who sports in the Self, rejoices in the Self, and is active in spiritual works—he is the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman. (3.1.4)

This one who is the "breath of breath," the Supreme Lord previously mentioned, shines—that is, He blazes forth in manifold ways—abiding in all beings, meaning He exists as the Self of all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass (the instrumental case here indicating a characteristic). The wise man who knows Him thus, directly as his own Self, thinking "I am this," by the mere knowledge of the meaning of that statement, becomes an *ativādī*. What does he overstate? He is so called because it is his habit (*śīla*) to speak beyond all others. He does not merely say "he exists" or "he does not exist"; rather, he transcends all other modes of speech.

The meaning is that he who, knowing the Self thus as the "breath of breath," is not an "exceeding speaker" (*ativādī*). When everything is seen as the Self alone and nothing else exists, what indeed would he speak by exceeding? Only one for whom another thing exists as something separate speaks by exceeding it. But this knower does not see anything other than the Self; he does not hear anything else, nor does he cognize anything else. Therefore, he does not speak by exceeding.

Furthermore, "one who sports in the Self" (*ātmakrīḍa*) means one whose play or sporting is in the Self alone and not elsewhere, such as in children, wife, and so forth. Likewise, "one who delights in the Self" (*ātmarati*) means one whose delight, enjoyment, or affection is in the Self alone. The distinction is that *krīḍā* (sporting) depends on external means, whereas *rati* (delight) is independent of means and consists merely of affection for external objects. Similarly, "one who possesses action" (*kriyāvān*) refers to one who possesses actions such as knowledge, meditation, and dispassion.

Regarding the compound reading, since the possessive suffix (*matup*) is already implied by the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself—meaning "one for whom the action of delighting in the Self exists"—either the suffix or the compound would be redundant. Thus, one of the two is superfluous.

Some, however, desire that there be a combination (*samuccaya*) of ritual acts such as the *agnihotra* and the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). But this contradicts the statement of primary significance: "He is the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman. For one who possesses external activity cannot be one who sports in the Self and finds delight in the Self; indeed, only one who has desisted from external activity becomes one who sports in the Self, because of the mutual opposition between external activity and sporting in the Self. For it is not possible for darkness and light to exist simultaneously in the same place.

Therefore, this demonstration of the combination of knowledge and action is merely the prattle of the ignorant. This is also evident from such scriptural passages as, "Abandon other words," and "By the yoga of renunciation. Consequently, he alone is truly an "actor" (*kriyāvān*) in this context who, while being a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*), possesses the actions of knowledge, meditation, and so forth, and does not transgress the noble boundaries of conduct. He who is characterized thus—one who does not speak excessively, who sports in the Self, who finds delight in the Self, who is an actor, and who is established in Brahman—he is the most excellent, the foremost among all knowers of Brahman. (3.1.4)
Now, the means of attainment—truth and so forth—which are primarily characterized by renunciation and act as auxiliaries to right knowledge for the mendicant, are prescribed:

"By truth, by austerity, by right knowledge, and by constant celibacy, this auspicious Self, consisting of light within the body, is attained; indeed, the ascetics whose defects have been destroyed perceive it. (3.1.5)

He is to be attained—that is, reached—through truth (*satya*), which consists in the abandonment of falsehood (*mṛṣāvāda*). Furthermore, through austerity (*tapas*), meaning through one-pointedness of the senses and the mind, for there is a traditional teaching (*smṛti*) stating: "The supreme austerity is indeed the one-pointedness of the mind and the senses. This austerity is the supreme means because it is conducive to being directed toward the vision of the Self; it is not other forms of austerity such as the *cāndrāyaṇa*. The phrase "this Self is to be attained" is to be supplied in every instance.

By right knowledge—that is, by seeing the Self as it truly is—by celibacy, which is the non-practice of sexual intercourse, always, at all times; [the word] "always" is to be supplied everywhere with the logic of the "internal lamp" (*antardīpikā-nyāya*), as in the phrases "always by truth," "always by austerity," and "always by right knowledge. And the author will later state: "In whom there is no crookedness, no falsehood, and no deceit."

What is this Self that is said to be attainable by these means? Indeed, within the body, in the space within the lotus-like heart, there is a Self consisting of light, golden-hued, brilliant, and pure—whom ascetics (yatayaḥ), those habituated to disciplined effort, namely renunciants (saṃnyāsinaḥ) whose defects have perished and whose mental impurities such as anger have been destroyed, perceive and realize. That Self is always attained through the means of truth and so forth, and through renunciations; it is never attained by [mere] truth and the like [without renunciation]. This is an explanatory praise (arthavāda) intended to extol the means such as truth. (3.1.5)
Truth alone triumphs, not falsehood; by truth is the path leading to the gods spread out, by which the seers whose desires are fulfilled ascend to where that supreme treasure of truth resides. 3.1.6.

The meaning is that truth alone, and the speaker of truth alone, conquers; falsehood does not, nor the speaker of falsehood. For victory or defeat is not possible for truth and falsehood in isolation, independent of a person. It is well known in the world that the speaker of truth overcomes the speaker of falsehood, and not the reverse; therefore, it is established that truth is a powerful means of success.

Furthermore, it is understood from scripture as well that truth possesses the quality of being a superior means. How so? By means of truth—namely, by the established practice of speaking according to reality—the path called the "way of the gods" (devayāna) is extended, wide, and continuously set forth. By this path, indeed, the seers (ṛṣis), who possess vision, ascend and traverse; and where—that is, in which supreme ultimate reality (paramārthatattva)—there lies the supreme, most excellent treasure (nidhāna) belonging to truth, the highest means, which is to be attained and is deposited in the form of the goal of human life (puruṣārtha).
The treasure-trove exists there, and the path by which they proceed is spread out by truth; this is the connection with what precedes. ||3.1.6||
What is that, and what is its nature? It is said:

That is vast and divine, of inconceivable form; it shines forth, subtler than the subtlest. It is far, farther than the far, yet it is near here; it is hidden right here within the cave of the heart for those who see. (3.1.7)

And that Brahman under discussion is vast and great because it pervades everything, having truth and other qualities as its means of realization. It is divine, self-luminous, and because it is beyond the range of the senses, its form cannot even be conceived; thus, it is of inconceivable form. It is subtler than the subtle, such as the atom and so forth, for its subtlety is unsurpassed due to its being the cause of all things. It shines forth, appearing in various forms such as the sun, the moon, and so on, and it blazes with light.

Moreover, that Brahman exists far away, in a remote place, even in a more distant place, because it is utterly inaccessible to the ignorant; yet it is also near here, in the vicinity of the body, because it is the Self of the wise. And because it is within all, it is also within space, as is heard in the scriptures. It is "hidden" (nihitam)—meaning situated—here among sentient beings who see, being perceived by yogins through their capacity for seeing and other such activities. Where? In the cave, characterized by the intellect; for there, hidden within, it is perceived by the wise.
Nevertheless, being shrouded by ignorance, it is not perceived by the ignorant, even though it resides right there. ||3.1.7||
Furthermore, that unique means of perceiving It is stated:

"It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by other gods, nor by austerity or ritual action. But one whose being is purified through the clarity of knowledge beholds That partless One while meditating upon It. (3.1.8)

Since it is not grasped by the eye because it is formless, nor is it grasped by speech because it is inexpressible, nor by other gods—that is, by the other sense organs—and although austerity is a means for attaining everything, it is not grasped by austerity; likewise, it is not grasped even by Vedic rites such as the Agnihotra, which are renowned for their greatness—what then is the means for its apprehension? He says:

By the clarity of knowledge (*jñānaprasāda*). Although the innate knowledge of all living beings is by nature capable of awakening to the Self, it does not bring about that awakening because it is turbid, unpurified, and impure due to the defects of passion and other afflictions directed toward external objects; thus, even though the reality of the Self is eternally present, it fails to perceive it, like a mirror covered with grime or like agitated water.

When, however, this [knowledge] becomes clear, calm, and pure—like a mirror or still water—by removing the turbidity of stains such as passion produced through contact with the objects of the senses, then there occurs the "clarity of knowledge."

By that clarity of knowledge, one whose being is purified and whose inner organ is cleansed becomes fit to see Brahman; therefore, meditating—meaning reflecting with a one-pointed mind while withdrawing the senses and possessing the means such as truth—he beholds, sees, and perceives that Self which is partless, devoid of all distinctions of limbs. || 3.1.8 ||
He who perceives the Self in this way:

"This subtle Self is to be known by the mind, in whom the vital breath has entered fivefold; in whom, when purified, this Self manifests—the mind of all creatures being woven upon the vital breaths. (3.1.9)

This subtle atom (aṇu) is to be known by the mind through pure, absolute knowledge. Where is it? The meaning is that it is to be known by the mind in the heart, within that very body wherein the vital air (prāṇa) has fully entered (saṃviveśa), having entered correctly in its fivefold division as prāṇa, apāna, and so forth.

With what kind of mind should this be known? He says: by that [mind] through which the entire internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—the consciousness (*citta*) of all living beings together with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the senses—is woven and pervaded, just as milk is by its own creaminess or wood by fire. For it is well known in the world that the entire internal organ of living beings possesses consciousness; and when that consciousness is pure, being freed from the impurities of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth, this aforementioned Self manifests therein, meaning that the Self manifests itself specifically by its own nature. (3.1.9)

To one who has realized the Self, characterized as described above, as the Self of all—precisely because of that state of being the Self of all—the scripture declares the fruit, which consists in the attainment of everything:

"Whatever world a person of purified being contemplates in his mind, and whatever desires he longs for, he is born into that world and obtains those desires; therefore, one who desires prosperity should indeed honor the knower of the Self. (3.1.10)

Whatever world characterized by fathers and so forth a person of pure being—one whose afflictions are exhausted, who knows the Self, and whose internal organ is stainless—visualizes with the mind, intending "may this be for me" or "for another," and whatever objects of desire he longs for and prays for, he conquers and attains that very world and those intended objects of enjoyment.

Therefore, one who desires prosperity—that is, one desiring worldly success—should worship and honor the wise man whose internal organ has been purified by the knowledge of the Self, because of his possession of the power of true resolve, through such acts as washing his feet, service, and prostration; for he is indeed worthy of worship. 3.1.10.
Thus ends the first section;
the second section begins from where it was left off.

He knows this supreme abode of Brahman, wherein the universe is deposited and shines forth in its purity. Those wise ones who, free from desire, worship that Puruṣa, they indeed transcend this radiant realm. 3.2.1.

He knows—that is, he realizes—that Brahman, which possesses the characteristics described above, is the supreme, most excellent abode (*dhāma*), the locus and support of all desires; in that Brahman-abode the entire universe is deposited and entrusted, and it shines by its own light, pure and stainless. Those who, being free from desire and devoid of thirst for worldly power, worship—that is, serve like a supreme deity—that person who knows the Self as such, they [attain] this well-known *śukra*, the seed of man.

The wise, the intelligent, transcend—that is, they go beyond—the material causes of the body; they do not enter a womb again, according to the Vedic scripture: "He takes no delight anywhere again. Therefore, the intention is that one should honor him. 3.2.1.
It is shown that for one who desires liberation, the renunciation of desire alone is the primary means:

"He who, thinking [of them], desires desires, is born through those desires here and there. But for one whose desires are fulfilled and whose self is perfected, all desires dissolve away right here. (3.2.2)

He who desires objects of sense—whether seen or unseen—desiring them by reflecting upon their qualities and yearning for them, is born together with those desires, which are the causes for the engagement in dharma and adharma and consist of the longing for sense-objects; wherever desires impel a person toward actions as a means to obtain objects, there, in those very objects, he is born enveloped by those same desires.

But for one who has attained all desires through the knowledge of the reality of the supreme truth—meaning one for whom all desires are completely fulfilled by the state of desiring the Self—for such a person who has attained all desires, and for one who has made himself "perfected" (*kṛtātman*) by means of knowledge, having removed the self from its other form characterized by ignorance and established it in its own supreme form; for him, even while remaining right here in this body, all causes for the engagement in dharma and adharma dissolve, go to dissolution, and perish—this is the meaning.
The intention is that desires do not arise because their cause, which is birth, has been destroyed. || 3.2.2 ||

If this is so, and since the attainment of the Self is the highest of all attainments, it follows that one should employ many means from the sacred teaching (pravacana) for its acquisition; to this it is replied:
This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing. Only he whom this [Self] chooses, by him is it attained; to him this Self reveals its own form. (3.2.3)

This Self which has been explained—the attainment of which is the supreme human goal—is not obtainable through the abundance of Vedic study or through extensive exposition. Likewise, it is not obtained through *medhā*, the power of retaining the meaning of texts, nor even through much *śruta*, meaning through excessive hearing. By what, then, is it obtained? It is said: this very Supreme Self is obtained by that very choice (*vara*) whereby the wise man chooses (*vṛṇute*)—that is, desires to attain—Him; not by any other means, because its nature is eternally attained.

What is this "attainment of the Self" (ātmalābha) for the wise? It is said: when knowledge exists, it reveals—that is, makes manifest—the very highest body of that [Self], which is its own true essence (svātmatattva) and its own nature (svarūpa), just as light reveals a jar or similar object; though that [essence] was previously concealed by ignorance. Therefore, the meaning is that the very seeking of the attainment of the Self through the renunciation of everything else is the means for attaining the Self. (3.2.3)
These means—strength, vigilance, and austerity, accompanied by the marks [of renunciation] and joined with renunciation—serve as aids to the soul's own aspiration. For it is said:

"This Self is not attained by one devoid of strength, nor through negligence, nor even through austerity without the marks. But for him who strives by these means, this Self, having pierced [the gates], enters the abode of Brahman. (3.2.4)

Because this Self cannot be attained by one who is devoid of strength—that is, by one who has lost his vigor due to a lack of self-reliance—nor by one who is negligent on account of attachment to worldly objects such as children and cattle, nor likewise by one whose austerity (*tapas*) is "without marks" (*aliṅga*), meaning devoid of the mark (*liṅga*) which is renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*); the meaning is that it is not attained through knowledge (*jñāna*) that is divorced from renunciation. But for that wise man, the discerning knower of the Self, who strives with these means—strength, vigilance, renunciation, and knowledge—being intent upon them, this Self enters into, fully penetrates, the abode of Brahman. 3.2.4.

How does one enter into Brahman? It is said: "The seers, satisfied with knowledge, perfected in self, free from passion, and tranquil; having reached that omnipresent One everywhere, those wise ones, with disciplined minds, enter into the All. (3.2.5)

Having fully attained and thoroughly understood this Self, those seers who possess true vision are satisfied by that very knowledge and not by external means of satisfaction which cause the nourishment of the body; having perfected themselves as the very nature of the Supreme Self, they become free from passion—meaning their defects such as passion and the like have vanished—and are tranquil with their senses withdrawn.

Those who have become such, having reached that which is all-pervading, all-encompassing, and like space—reaching it not through a limited portion defined by adjuncts (*upādhi*), but rather by realizing that very non-dual Brahman as their own Self—the wise ones, who are utterly discerning, whose minds are disciplined, and whose nature is eternally composed, enter into the entirety of everything even at the time of the body's fall; they cast off the limitation created by adjuncts produced by ignorance, just as the space within a jar [is not lost] when the jar is broken. Thus, the knowers of Brahman enter the abode of Brahman. (3.2.5)
Moreover:

"Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta, who are self-controlled through the yoga of renunciation, and whose being is purified—they, having become supreme immortality at the time of the final end, are all liberated in the worlds of Brahman. (3.2.6)

"Vedānta-vijñāna" is the wisdom born of the Vedanta; its "object" (artha) is the Supreme Self (paramātman), which is to be known. Those for whom that object is well-ascertained are "those whose object is well-ascertained through the wisdom of Vedanta. And they, by means of the yoga of renunciation—which is characterized by the abandonment of all actions—and by the yoga consisting of the nature of exclusive devotion to Brahman, are "strivers" (yatayaḥ), meaning those whose habit is effort. They are "pure in essence" (śuddhasattvāḥ), meaning those whose internal being (sattva) has become pure through the yoga of renunciation.

They [reside] in the worlds of Brahman—referring to the time of the final end (parānta) of transmigrating beings at death, as opposed to the time of abandoning the body at the conclusion of worldly existence for those seeking liberation.

The "time of the ultimate end" (*parāntakāla*) refers to that time when, due to the great number of practitioners, Brahman itself is the world—the "Brahma-world" (*brahmaloka*). Although it is one, it is seen or attained as if it were many; therefore, the plural form "in the Brahma-worlds" (*brahmalokeṣu*) is used, meaning "in Brahman. Those who have attained the supreme nectar (*parāmṛtāḥ*)—that is, those for whom the supreme nectar, which is the immortal nature of Brahman, has become their very self—are "living-liberated" (*jīvanta eva brahmabhūtāḥ*). Being thus liberated by the supreme nectar, they are completely released on all sides, like the extinguishing of a lamp or the space within a jar.

They attain cessation; they are liberated, released on all sides, and none of them require traveling to another place. As stated in the Śruti and Smṛti: "Just as the track of birds in the sky or of aquatic creatures in the water cannot be seen, so too is the path of those possessed of knowledge"; and "Though not travelers, they reach the end of the paths."

For movement delimited by space pertains only to the realm of saṃsāra, because it is accomplished by means that are themselves spatially limited. Brahman, however, because it is all-pervading, cannot be reached by a movement restricted to a particular location. For if Brahman were delimited by space, it would—like material objects—be subject to beginning and end, dependent on something else, composed of parts, and non-eternal; yet Brahman cannot be of such a nature. Therefore, its attainment cannot logically be one that is spatially delimited.

Moreover, those who know Brahman desire liberation as nothing other than the removal of the bonds of saṃsāra, beginning with ignorance; they do not regard it as something produced as an effect. (3.2.6)
Moreover, at the time of liberation:

"The fifteen parts have returned to their foundations, and all the deities have returned to their respective deities; the works and the self consisting of consciousness all become one in the supreme Imperishable. (3.2.7)

The meaning is that those constituent parts (kalā) which initiate the body, such as the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth, go each to its own support; "support" (pratiṣṭhā) here is the accusative plural. Furthermore, the fifteen—the well-known deities enumerated in the final question, numbering fifteen, who reside in the body and are situated in the instruments such as the eyes—all go back to their respective deities. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, those actions performed by one desiring liberation whose fruits have not yet begun to manifest—since those whose fruits have already begun are exhausted solely through experience—the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), having mistaken the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the intellect created by ignorance for its own self, has entered here into various bodies, like the reflection of the sun in water and other surfaces, because action exists for the sake of its fruit; and thus, together with that very self consisting of consciousness, it is "consisting of consciousness," meaning it is predominantly consciousness.

When the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) are removed, these very actions, along with that self, become one in the Supreme Brahman—which is imperishable, undecaying, immortal, fearless, like space, without interior or exterior, without duality, auspicious, and tranquil—and they attain non-distinction; they reach oneness, just as reflections of the sun and other objects vanish into the sun when their support (the water) is removed, or as the space within a jar merges into the universal space when the jar is removed. || 3.2.7 ||
Moreover:
"Just as rivers flowing along reach the ocean and lose their names and forms, so the knower, freed from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high. (3.2.8)

Just as rivers flowing from the Gaṅgā go toward the ocean, and having reached the ocean, they attain disappearance and a state of non-distinction, casting off both name and form—so too the knower, being liberated from name and form created by ignorance, attains and reaches the divine Puruṣa beyond the aforementioned supreme Imperishable, whose characteristics have been described. 3.2.8.

[Objection: Surely it is well known that there are many obstacles to the highest good (*śreya*); therefore, even one who knows Brahman, being obstructed by any one of the afflictions (*kleśa*) or by some other agent such as a deity, would go to another destination upon death, and not to Brahman itself.

[Response: No; because by knowledge alone all obstructions are removed. For liberation is merely the removal of the obstruction of ignorance (*avidyā*), and not the removal of any other obstruction, since [liberation] is eternal and constitutes the very nature of the Self (*ātman*).
Therefore—

He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself; in his family there shall be no one ignorant of Brahman. He crosses over sorrow, he crosses over evil, and being liberated from the knots of the heart, he becomes immortal. 3.2.9.

Whoever in this world truly knows that supreme Brahman as "I am indeed That," he does not go to any other state. Even the gods cannot create an obstacle for him regarding the attainment of Brahman, for he becomes their very Self. Therefore, the knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself.

Furthermore, for this wise one, there is no [rebirth] in the family of those who know Brahman. Moreover, he crosses over sorrow—that mental anguish caused by the deficiency of many desired objects—and even while living, he has transcended it. He crosses over evil, known as merit and demerit (dharma and adharma). Being liberated from the knots of the cave—the knots of ignorance in the heart—he becomes immortal; this has already been stated in such passages as, "The knot of the heart is broken," and so forth. 3.2.9.
Now, the conclusion is made by demonstrating the rule for the transmission of the knowledge of Brahman. This very point has been declared in a Ṛgvedic verse:

"To those who perform the rites, who are learned in the Vedas, who are firmly established in Brahman, who themselves offer oblations to the Single Seer with faith, and who have duly observed the vow of the head—only to them should one impart this knowledge of Brahman. (3.2.10)
This very procedure for the transmission of knowledge is declared and illuminated by a verse, that is, by a mantra:

To those who are performers of action—meaning those engaged in the performance of prescribed duties, learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), established in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭha*), devoted to the lower Brahman while desiring to know the Supreme Brahman—who themselves offer oblations into the fire named *ekarṣi* with faith, being full of devotion; to those very ones whose souls are purified and who have become fit vessels, one should declare this knowledge of Brahman. This applies to those by whom the "head-vow" (*śirovrata*)—characterized by carrying fire upon the head—is observed, just as the Vedic vow of the Atharvans is well known. And by whomsoever... [the text continues].
And that was practiced by them according to the rule, exactly as prescribed.
This truth was formerly proclaimed by the seer Aṅgiras; one who has not observed his vows does not study this. Homage to the supreme seers! Homage to the supreme seers! 3.2.11.

This very Imperishable, the Person, the Truth, the sage named Aṅgiras spoke of old, in the past, to Śaunaka, who had approached him according to the prescribed rule and questioned him. The meaning is that anyone else as well should likewise speak it to one who has approached according to the rule for the sake of liberation, seeking the highest good and desiring release. This is not merely a book; one who has not observed his vows does not study or recite it. For knowledge, when belonging to one who has observed his vows, becomes refined and leads to its fruit.

The knowledge of Brahman is complete. Salutations to those supreme seers (paramarṣis) from whom it was received through the succession of tradition, beginning with Brahmā. Those such as Brahmā who have directly perceived and understood the Supreme Brahman are the supreme seers; to them, again, salutations.
The repetition is for the sake of showing extreme reverence and for the purpose of concluding the Muṇḍaka. 3.2.11.
Thus ends the second section;
this concludes the third Muṇḍaka.
